incident_details.title: High Risk Alerts: ESA for 192.168.10.14
incident_details.description: This alert shows network traffic from an internal host (192.168.10.14) to multicast/broadcast-style addresses (239.255.255.250 and 255.255.255.255) with no evidence of PowerShell, endpoint activity, file transfer, or exfiltration. Based on the available telemetry and low IOC confidence, this appears to be a network anomaly rather than confirmed malicious activity.

gap_findings.step_1: Identify 1. username 2. IP addre: The incident data only provides a source IP of 192.168.10.14 and broadcast/multicast destinations (239.255.255.250, 255.255.255.255), which is consistent with local-network discovery or noisy broadcast activity rather than a confirmed user logon. No username, authentication detail, hostname, or OS is present in the alert record. The source IP is in RFC1918 private space and suggests an internal host on the 192.168.10.0/24 network, but the endpoint identity remains unresolved.
gap_findings.step_2: Was it horizontal or vertical: The available network evidence points away from clear lateral movement. The only destination addresses are 239.255.255.250 (SSDP/UPnP multicast used for service discovery) and 255.255.255.255 (limited broadcast), which are not evidence of host-to-host pivoting. Because there is no distinct remote internal target IP, no subnet-to-subnet movement, and no authentication trail to another machine, this is not enough to call horizontal or vertical movement. The most defensible assessment is that movement type is not established; if anything, the pattern is more consistent with local discovery/broadcast activity than lateral movement.
gap_findings.step_3: Was any malicious process spawne: No process data, parent-child lineage, command line, or EDR telemetry is included in the incident record, so there is no direct evidence that a malicious process spawned on the victim machine. The alert is network/event-stream based and only shows IP-level activity. Therefore, malicious process execution on the endpoint is not present in the provided data.
gap_findings.step_4: Analyze the process tree for sig: A process tree cannot be analyzed from the available evidence because no process names, parent/child relationships, command lines, hashes, services, scheduled tasks, or shell activity are provided. There are also no indicators of privilege escalation or data exfiltration in the alert metadata. The observable behavior is limited to internal source IP 192.168.10.14 generating traffic to broadcast/multicast addresses, which more strongly resembles discovery/noisy network behavior than explicit malicious execution. If compromise is suspected, the missing process tree evidence would be necessary before any conclusion about escalation, movement, or exfiltration can be made.

actionable_queries.step_1: Identify 1. username 2. IP addre: Query Windows Security Logs on the endpoint for Event ID 4624/4625 to identify usernames, logon type, source IP, and logon timestamps; query Event ID 4634/4647 for logoff context; query Event ID 4688 for process creation with user context; query System/Computer inventory via EDR or Active Directory to map 192.168.10.14 to hostname and OS; if available, inspect DHCP lease logs, DNS records, or EDR host metadata for computer name and operating system.
actionable_queries.step_2: Was it horizontal or vertical: Query Windows Security Event ID 4624/4625 on 192.168.10.14 and any candidate destination hosts to identify remote logons; query Event ID 5140/5145 for SMB share access and Event ID 4776/4768/4769 for authentication activity; use EDR network telemetry to identify whether 192.168.10.14 connected to another internal host in the same /24 or different subnet. For command-line validation on the host, run netstat -ano and arp -a; if EDR supports it, search for connections from 192.168.10.14 to non-broadcast internal IPs.
actionable_queries.step_3: Was any malicious process spawne: Query Windows Security Event ID 4688 (process creation) and Sysmon Event ID 1 for the time window around 2025-07-15T07:28:57Z; collect EDR process execution telemetry, including command line, parent process, hash, and signer; on the endpoint run Get-Process, wmic process list full, and tasklist /v to inspect active processes; review PowerShell logs Event ID 4104 and service-install logs Event ID 7045 for execution artifacts.
actionable_queries.step_4: Analyze the process tree for sig: Query Sysmon Event ID 1 (process creation), 3 (network connections), 10 (process access), 11 (file creation), and 13/14 (registry modifications) to reconstruct process lineage; query Windows Security Event ID 4688, 4672 (special privileges assigned), 4697/7045 (service creation), 4698 (scheduled task creation), and 4104 (PowerShell script block logging); use EDR to pull full process tree, command lines, hashes, and child process relationships; if data exfiltration is suspected, review proxy/firewall logs and DNS logs for large outbound transfers or suspicious external destinations.
